question: A 56-year-old man comes to the physician because of intermittent retrosternal chest pain. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Endoscopy shows salmon pink mucosa extending 5 cm proximal to the gastroesophageal junction. Biopsy specimens from the distal esophagus show nonciliated columnar epithelium with numerous goblet cells. Which of the following is the most likely cause of this patient's condition?

options.ope: Fungal infection of the lower esophagus

reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Esophageal exposure to gastric acid -> Chronic irritation of the esophageal mucosa -> Metaplasia of the esophageal epithelium -> Barrett's esophagus -> Salmon pink mucosa with goblet cells -> Esophageal exposure to gastric acid is the most likely cause -> 95%
enhanced_information: Esophageal exposure to gastric acid can lead to chronic irritation and metaplasia of the esophageal epithelium, eventually resulting in Barrett's esophagus characterized by salmon pink mucosa with goblet cells. The most likely cause of this patient's condition is esophageal exposure to gastric acid, leading to Barrett's esophagus.
analysis: Barrett's esophagus is a condition characterized by the replacement of normal squamous epithelium with columnar epithelium containing goblet cells, typically due to chronic exposure to gastric acid. In this case, the patient's presentation of retrosternal chest pain, salmon pink mucosa, and goblet cells on biopsy align with Barrett's esophagus secondary to esophageal exposure to gastric acid.
